I forget who discovered what the problem was. In any case it's an infection rarely seen these days what with pasteurized milk. Brucellosis/Bang's Disease/Undulant Fever. It has several names, and it's caused by a bacterium that is killed by pasteurization. Nowadays it's rarely seen except in farmers, veterinarians and meat plant workers. Most physicians will go through their entire career without seeing it even though it was much more common in the past.

This is one of those issues that I think is a lot more complex than it seems at first glance. Yes, the kid died due to these parents' inaction and that is terrible.

On the other hand, attempting to prevent that inaction could lead to some pretty dark situations in its own right from a personal liberty perspective.

To prevent this - the government would have needed to at minimum apply some level of treatment to the child with the express lack of consent of their parents. For meningitis I believe this can include actually cutting the skull to relieve pressure which to my layman's ears sounds pretty invasive.

It's easy to light up the pitchforks in this case because we know the outcome of this solution - the child dies, and it's often a reasonably survivable disease with prompt treatment (again - from internets, not a doctor). The trouble comes in where to draw the line.

What is negligence of not getting a specific treatment - what treatment is a sure thing with no risks. What if the government had took custody of the child - performed procedures on the child and the child died due to complications?

Finally - who makes these calls? We've seen plenty of examples of courts and experts being coerced in one way or another and completely losing any of the oversight they were supposed to provide. What would stop this precident from being applied to things that really are nefarious in a tinfoil hat sense?
